title: The Exchange: 3.exd5
intro:
White releases the tension straight away. After 3...cxd5 the pawns are symmetrical, the position is level, and both sides simply develop. This is the quietest chapter in the course and the one you are most likely to see from an opponent who does not know the Caro-Kann.

## Recapture with the c-pawn

3...cxd5 is automatic. It keeps a pawn on d5, opens the c-file for a rook and leaves the bishop on c8 free to come out. Taking with the queen instead invites 4.Nc3, which develops a piece and gains a move on her.

## What Black is playing for

The half open c-file. Black's rook belongs on c8, the knight on c6, and the pressure builds against c2 and the b-file. White has the same file on the other side and one extra move, so this is not a position to force. Develop properly, castle, put the rook on c8 and the position plays itself.

## The one line worth knowing

After 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 Bg4 White often plays 7.Qb3, hitting b7 and looking at d5. The answer is 7...Na5, chasing the queen and covering everything at once. After 8.Qa4+ Bd7 9.Qc2 Black has gained time and stands perfectly well. Learn that one sequence and the rest of the chapter is common sense.

## Not this chapter

If White follows up with 4.c4 the game becomes the Panov, which is chapter 4. It is a completely different sort of position, so do not treat 4.c4 as a sideline of this chapter.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Recapturing with the queen and losing a move to Nc3. Answering 7.Qb3 by defending b7 with the queen, which leaves Black passive when ...Na5 solves everything. Trading on f3 without a reason and handing White the bishop pair. And treating a symmetrical position as a draw, then drifting: the c-file is a real asset if a rook is put on it.

tree.note: Recapture with the c-pawn. It keeps a pawn on d5, opens the c-file and leaves the bishop free.

mistakes.note: 4.Nc3 develops a piece and hits the queen, so White gets a free move. This is a Scandinavian, and a poor version of one.

children.note: The main move. White eyes h7 and keeps the c-pawn free for c3.
Develop towards the centre and put a second attacker on d4.

mistakes.note: Also good, and it usually transposes. The queenside knight is the one with an obvious square.
There is nothing on f3 to pin, and the queen sees g4: 5.Qxg4 simply wins the bishop.

children.note: The standard setup. White props up d4 and gives the queen the c2 square.
Develop and cover e4 and d5.

mistakes.note: A perfectly sound setup with ...Bg7. It is a different plan and it gives up on the quick ...Bg4.
Solid, but it shuts in the bishop on c8 before it has been given a square.

children.note: White develops the last minor piece to its best diagonal.
Out it comes, before ...e6 has to be played. The bishop takes aim at the squares White needs for the knight.

mistakes.note: Solid, but it locks in the bishop on c8 for no reason. Getting it out first is the whole idea of the opening.
It is not a trade: 7.Bxf5 simply wins the bishop, because with no pawn on e6 and none on g6 nothing takes back. On g4 the bishop is safe.

children.note: The critical try. The queen hits b7 and takes a look at d5.
The move to remember. It attacks the queen and keeps b7 covered by getting out of the way of the rook.

mistakes.note: It defends b7 and leaves Black passive with the queen tied down. ...Na5 solves the same problem and gains time.
8.Qxb7 wins the pawn and hits the rook on a8 at the same time, so Black loses time as well. The move guards d5 and forgets what the queen came out for.

children.note: The queen keeps the check available and steps away from the knight.
Block with the bishop, gaining another move on the queen.

mistakes.note: It undoes the last move and invites a repetition where White is the one with a choice.

children.note: The queen comes back to the useful diagonal.
Now the pawn can come. The bishop is already outside on d7 and has done its job.

mistakes.note: The knight looks active and 10.Bxc4 dxc4 leaves Black with a weak pawn and no compensation.

children.note: White finally develops the kingside knight.
Quiet development. Note that 10...Bd6 would simply hang a piece: the bishop on d7 blocks the queen, so nothing recaptures after 11.Bxd6.

mistakes.note: It looks like the usual trade offer and it drops a bishop. 11.Bxd6 cannot be answered, because the queen on d8 is shut in by Black's own bishop on d7.

children.plan: Castle, then put a rook on c8 and bring the knight back from a5 through c4 or c6. Black has gained two moves on the queen and stands at least equal.
children.name: The full main line, with 7.Qb3

children.note: Quiet development, accepting that the bishop on g4 is there.
Complete the structure. The bishop is already outside, so nothing is shut in.

mistakes.note: It gives White the two bishops for no return. Keep the tension until White does something about it.

children.note: White castles into a quiet, level position.
Offer the trade. Swapping dark-squared bishops suits Black, whose remaining pieces have clear squares.
White takes rather than retreat.
Recapture with the queen, which now eyes the kingside and supports ...e5 one day.
children.plan: Castle short, put a rook on c8 and think about ...e5 once the pieces are out. The position is level and there is nothing to be afraid of.
children.name: 7.Nf3 instead of the queen check

children.note: Development first, leaving the c-pawn where it is for now.
Develop and keep every option open.

mistakes.note: Fine too, though 6.h3 asks the question immediately and Black has to decide about taking on f3.

children.note: White spends a move to keep the bishop off g4.
With g4 taken away the bishop has no outside square, so the structure comes first and the bishop goes to d7 later.

mistakes.note: It does not get the bishop out, it gives it away: 7.Bxf5 and nothing recaptures, with no pawn on e6 and none on g6. Play ...e6 first.

children.note: White castles.
Get ready to castle and take the diagonal aimed at h2.
children.plan: Castle, play ...Rc8 or ...Bd7 and ...Rc8, and look for ...Ne4 or the ...e5 break once the pieces are all out.
children.name: 5.Nf3 before c3

children.note: The pawn to b3 before castling, the Colle-Zukertort course's move: it reaches this structure by 1.d4 c5 2.e3 cxd4 3.exd4 d5 and puts the bishop on b2.

The bishop to d6, as in every line of this chapter: it looks at h2, and the bishop that is going to b2 looks at nothing while the pawn on d4 blocks it. The Colle course expects ...Be7 here and this is the better square.

mistakes.note: Sound, and the move the Colle course lists. On d6 the bishop does more.
Sound and the engine's choice: 8.O-O Bb7 9.c3 Bd6 and the same setup with both bishops out. The bishop first.
Sound: 8.Be2 Bd6 9.O-O O-O and the knight has hit the bishop for nothing.

children.plan: ...O-O, ...b6 and ...Bb7, ...Re8 and ...Ne4 when the knight on f3 is the only piece holding it. Level, with the bishop on d6 the better of the two dark bishops.
children.name: 5.Nf3 before c3, with 7.b3

children.note: The Panov. White strikes at d5 straight away and the game changes character completely.
Develop and defend d5. This is the start of chapter 4.
children.plan: Go to chapter 4. In short: 5.Nc3 e6 and Black blockades the isolated pawn White ends up with after cxd5.
children.name: 4.c4, into the Panov

children.note: A check for its own sake. It gains no time once the knight blocks.
Block with a developing move. The knight was going there anyway.

mistakes.note: Also fine, and it invites the trade on d7. Blocking with the knight develops the piece that has fewer squares.
It blocks the bishop on c8 and leaves the knight on a worse square than c6.

children.note: Development, and the knight supports d4.
Out and active, pinning the knight against the queen.
White asks the question.
Take. White has to recapture with the queen or wreck the pawns, and the knight on f3 was the main defender of d4.

mistakes.note: 7.g4 Bg6 8.Ne5 gains time and space, and the bishop ends up doing nothing.

children.note: The natural recapture, keeping the structure whole.
Solid. The bishop that mattered has been traded and Black has an easy game.
children.plan: Play ...Bd6, castle and put a rook on c8. White's bishop on b5 will have to move again, which is another move Black gains.
children.name: The 4.Bb5+ check

children.note: Development, keeping every setup available.
The usual square, hitting d4.

mistakes.note: Perfectly good and it pins the knight. Developing the knight first keeps ...Bg4 for the moment White commits the bishop.

children.note: White returns to the main setup.
Develop and cover d5 and e4, exactly as in the main line.
children.plan: This is the main line of this chapter by a different order. Expect 6.h3 e6 7.O-O Bd6, or 6.c3 Bg4 with the ...Na5 idea against Qb3.
children.name: The plain 4.Nf3

children.note: The bishop out first, the London player's habit: the London course reaches this structure by 1.d4 c5 2.e3 cxd4 3.exd4 d5 and plays exactly this.

Develop, the move the London course expects. The bishop on f4 has taken the square the knight on c6 would have hit, so the plan is ...Nc6 and ...Bg4 as against 4.Bd3, with ...Qb6 hitting b2 once the bishop has left c1.

mistakes.note: Sound and the engine's choice: 5.Nf3 Bg4 6.c3 e6 and the same setup. The knight on f6 first meets the London course on its own ground.
Sound: 5.c4 and the centre opens with the bishop out. The knight first.
5.Nc3 and the pawn on b2 is held by nothing but the queen has no follow-up: 5...Qxb2 6.Nb5 and the queen is in trouble.

children.note: The knight, and the London course's line ends here.
The knight to c6, hitting d4, and ...Bg4 or ...Bf5 next. With the bishop on f4 the queen on d8 sees b6, and ...Qb6 comes when c3 has been played and b2 is loose.

mistakes.note: Sound: 6.c3 e6 and the same setup with the bishop out first.
Sound: 6.Nc3 Bd7 7.Qd2 e6 and the pawn on b2 is held. The knight first.
It shuts the bishop on c8 in before it has chosen f5 or g4.

children.plan: ...Bf5 or ...Bg4, ...e6 and ...Bd6 to trade the bishop on f4, ...Qb6 when c3 has left b2 loose. The Exchange structure with White's bishop already committed.
children.name: 4.Bf4, the London player's bishop
